An uncrewed submarine launched from the research ship Halcyon has mapped a field of more than forty hydrothermal vents in a deep valley west of the Kestrel Ridge, an area that existing charts showed as flat, featureless seabed.

The vents, some of them taller than a two-storey house, release water heated to more than 300 degrees Celsius by rock beneath the ocean floor. Minerals dissolved in that water settle as it cools, building chimneys that grow by several centimetres a year.

A survey that changed course

The expedition, led by marine geologists at the University of Northmere, had set out to measure currents along the ridge. When temperature sensors on the submarine picked up a faint warm plume, the team spent two extra days following it downhill.

"We were looking at the screen at three in the morning and the temperature kept climbing. Nobody went to bed that night," said Dr Mirela Constantin, the expedition's chief scientist.

The submarine flew a lawnmower pattern fifty metres above the valley floor, building a sonar map with a resolution of about one metre. It then dropped closer to photograph the largest chimneys and to collect water samples from three of them.

Life in the dark

Early images show dense mats of bacteria, pale crabs and clusters of tube worms around several vents. Animals at hydrothermal vents live without sunlight, relying instead on microbes that draw energy from chemicals in the hot water.

Biologists on the team say that at least two of the crab species do not match any described so far, although confirming that will take months of work on the samples now travelling back to port in refrigerated containers.

Because vents are often rich in copper, zinc and rare metals, they have drawn interest from deep-sea mining companies. Dr Constantin said that the new map should be used to protect the site. "Places like this are rare and slow to recover. We have only just found it, and we know almost nothing about what lives here."

The full map and the first set of photographs will be published in an open-access data archive next month, and the team hopes to return to the valley with a crewed submersible in 2028.
